kurz: How price, down payment, interest rate and term turn into a monthly payment, a balance and a total interest bill, what mortgage insurance costs and when refinancing pays off.

bloecke.md:
When you buy a home with a loan, you sign a promissory note and a mortgage or deed of trust that run for up to 30 years in addition to the purchase contract. The house is often chosen over months, whereas the loan is frequently chosen in an afternoon. Yet clear rules apply to the loan, and it offers more scope for influencing the costs.

All the calculations in this lesson relate to the same case. The house costs $400,000. The buyer pays $12,000 in closing costs and puts down 20%, so the mortgage amounts to $320,000. The interest rate is assumed at 6.25% for a 30-year fixed-rate loan. It is an assumption for illustration, not a quote; Freddie Mac publishes the weekly national average in its Primary Mortgage Market Survey. Offers also state an annual percentage rate (APR), which adds points and certain fees to the interest rate and is therefore the better figure for comparing offers.

bloecke.md:
## Term and composition of the payment

In the US, the payment is calculated from the term. The 30-year term is the standard, and 15- and 20-year terms are common alternatives. The payment of $1,970.30 stays the same for 30 years, but its composition changes. In the first year, $19,894 goes to the lender as interest and only $3,750 into principal. In the tenth year, it is still $17,072 interest and $6,571 principal. Only in the 228th month, that is, in the 19th year, does principal exceed interest for the first time. The principal portion grows each year by roughly the interest rate, because no more interest is charged on each dollar repaid. This is the same compound interest effect as with saving, except that here it lowers interest costs instead of increasing income.

bloecke.titel: Interest and principal portions of the payment in selected years
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for $320,000 at 6.25% over 30 years; the bars are the same height, and only from the 19th year does principal exceed interest.

Illustrative calculation with the same loan amount and, for comparison, the same interest rate; after ten years, the balance with a 30-year and with a 15-year term differs by around $128,500. In practice, 15-year loans usually carry a lower rate, which widens the gap.

bloecke.titel: Cost and effect of the term ($320,000, 6.25%)

bloecke.md: A 15-year term instead of 30 years costs $773.45 more a month at the same rate. In return, the loan is paid off 15 years earlier, and the total interest falls by around $215,000. A low payment therefore extends the period in which interest is charged and increases the total cost. The 30-year loan has one advantage, however: it keeps the required payment low, and extra payments can still be made voluntarily.

## The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage

The typical US mortgage combines two features that are rare internationally. The rate is fixed for the entire term, and the borrower may repay the loan early at any time. Since 2014, federal rules have prohibited prepayment penalties on most residential mortgages; where they are still allowed, on certain fixed-rate loans, they are limited to the first three years and to at most 2% of the amount prepaid (12 CFR 1026.43(g)). This combination is possible mainly because most loans are sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac or insured by government agencies and then securitized, so the interest rate risk lies with investors in mortgage-backed securities instead of with the lender.

For the borrower, this means no refinancing risk: the payment for principal and interest is known to the cent for 30 years. If rates fall, the borrower can refinance; if they rise, the old rate continues to apply. This one-sided option is not free. It is priced into the interest rate. Loans that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy must stay within the conforming loan limit, which FHFA set at $832,750 for a one-unit home in most areas for 2026, with higher limits in high-cost areas. Larger loans are called jumbo loans and are subject to each lender's own requirements.

bloecke.md:
## Down payment and mortgage insurance

The **loan-to-value ratio** (LTV) relates the loan amount to the lower of the purchase price and the appraised value. A down payment of less than 20%, that is, an LTV above 80%, usually requires mortgage insurance on a conventional loan. It protects the lender, not the borrower, and the borrower pays for it. Freddie Mac gives an order of magnitude of $30 to $70 a month for every $100,000 borrowed; the actual premium depends above all on credit score and down payment.

Under the Homeowners Protection Act of 1998, private mortgage insurance on a conventional loan does not run forever. You can request cancellation once the balance is scheduled to reach, or through extra payments has reached, 80% of the original value of the home, provided you have a good payment history and the property has not lost value; the lender may require an appraisal. The insurance ends automatically when the balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the original value, and at the latest at the midpoint of the term. FHA mortgage insurance follows different rules and, with less than 10% down, can only be removed by refinancing.

bloecke.titel: Three down payments for the same house (price $400,000, 6.25%, 30 years)

bloecke.md:
Illustrative calculation for $320,000 over 30 years.

- At 6.25%, the payment is $1,970.30, interest over the first ten years $185,996 and over the full term $389,306.
- At 6.50%, the payment is $2,022.62, interest $193,998 over ten years and $408,142 in total.
- At 6.75%, the payment is $2,075.51, interest $202,025 over ten years and $427,185 in total.

Each quarter point costs around $52 a month, $8,000 over ten years and $19,000 over the full term. A better credit score can move a borrower into a cheaper pricing tier. Discount points work the other way round: one point costs 1% of the loan, here $3,200. If it lowers the rate from 6.25% to 6.00%, an assumption, because how much a point lowers the rate differs by lender and day, the payment falls by $51.73 a month, and the point has paid for itself after about 62 months. Points only pay off for borrowers who keep the loan longer than that.

A buyer who puts down 3% or 5% and pays the closing costs from a lender credit starts with almost no equity. After selling costs of around 6%, the home would have to rise in value for years before a sale would cover the loan. If prices fall, the loan is underwater: the balance exceeds the value of the house, and a move or a refinance becomes difficult. The down payment therefore does more than lower the payment and the mortgage insurance. It is the buffer against a forced sale at a loss.

## Extra payments, shorter terms and recasting

Because most mortgages can be repaid early without a penalty, every extra payment of principal is allowed at any time. If the borrower in the example pays an extra $200 every month, the balance after ten years falls from $269,561 to $236,336. The loan is paid off after 23.5 years instead of 30, and the borrower saves around $99,000 in interest. Some servicers offer a recast: after a large extra payment, the payment is recalculated for the remaining term at the same rate, usually for a small fee. Without a recast, the payment stays the same and the loan simply ends earlier.

## Repaying or investing

Mortgage interest only reduces taxes for households that itemize deductions, and since the standard deduction was roughly doubled in 2018, most do not. For them, every dollar repaid earns a risk-free return equal to the interest rate, here 6.25%. An investment in a taxable account would have to earn this after tax. With long-term capital gains taxed at 15%, that is around 7.35% before tax, and without risk, which stocks cannot promise. Treasury securities are safe, but they would have to yield more than the mortgage rate.

Two things come before extra payments, however. The first is an [[Emergency fund|emergency fund]], because money that has gone into the house cannot be withdrawn without a new loan, and lenders tend to freeze or cut home equity lines of credit exactly when the economy weakens, as many did in 2008. The second is the full employer match in a 401(k), which is an immediate return that no mortgage rate can beat.

## Refinancing

A **rate-and-term refinance** replaces the existing loan with a new one at a lower rate or a different term. It is a complete new mortgage, with a new application, appraisal, Loan Estimate and closing costs, often several thousand dollars. A **cash-out refinance** also increases the loan and pays out part of the home equity. FHA and VA loans offer simplified streamline refinances.

Whether a refinance pays off can be calculated. Example: a loan of $320,000 taken out at 7.25% has a balance of $309,995 after three years and a payment of $2,182.96. A new 30-year loan at 6.00% lowers the payment to $1,858.57, a saving of $324.39 a month. With closing costs of $6,000, the refinance has paid for itself after about 19 months. The comparison of monthly payments overstates the gain, however, because the term starts again at 30 years. If the new loan is set to the remaining 27 years instead, the payment is $1,934.32 and the total interest still to be paid falls from about $397,000 to about $317,000, instead of to $359,000 with the new 30-year term.

bloecke.titel: Decision points during the life of a mortgage
bloecke.unter: Three events offer room for manoeuvre: falling rates, reaching 80% of the original value and spare cash. None of them requires an early repayment charge on most loans.

bloecke.titel: Cash-out refinances and home equity loans
bloecke.md: A cash-out refinance or a home equity line of credit turns home equity back into debt, and the house is the collateral. Paying off credit cards or a car loan this way lowers the interest rate, but it stretches short debts over 30 years and puts the home at risk if the payments cannot be made. A home equity line of credit usually has a variable rate, and the lender can freeze or reduce it if the home's value falls. Anyone who uses home equity as a reserve should not plan on it being available in a crisis.
